eras.title: Before the Göktürks
eras.intro: The interludes about older times: the first monuments and towns of Anatolia, its ancient cities, and customs with roots in antiquity. Turkic speakers reached Anatolia much later, from the 11th century.

eras.title: The Göktürks and the steppe
eras.intro: The name *Türk* enters written history in the 6th century, with a nomadic empire of Inner Asia far to the east of Anatolia. The timeline starts here.

eras.title: From the steppe to Anatolia
eras.intro: Turkic-speaking groups move west. The Seljuks take Iran and reach Anatolia, where a Seljuk sultanate rules much of the peninsula from Konya until the Mongols defeat it in 1243.

eras.title: The Ottoman centuries
eras.intro: Around 1300 Osman leads one of the small principalities of north-western Anatolia. His dynasty rules from Istanbul after 1453; defeated in the First World War, the empire signs the Armistice of Mudros in 1918.

eras.title: War of Independence and the Republic
eras.intro: From Mustafa Kemal's landing at Samsun in 1919 to the Republic proclaimed on 29 October 1923, its reforms, and the traditions alive today.

events.text: The Grand National Assembly adopts the law on the new Turkish letters on 1 November, and within months Turkish moves from the Ottoman script to a Latin alphabet of 29 letters.
Eye beads, the ancestors of the *nazar boncuğu*, survive from as early as the 16th century BCE. Today the blue beads are made in kilns at Görece and Nazarköy, near İzmir.
The Surname Law is adopted on 21 June and comes into force on 2 January 1935; until then most people in Turkey had no family name.
Tradition places Nasreddin Hoca in 13th-century Anatolia, in Sivrihisar and then Akşehir. The oldest text that mentions him was written around 1480.
Greek colonists from Megara found Byzantion on the Bosphorus. The city becomes Constantinople in 330, the Ottoman capital in 1453, and *İstanbul* is its only official name from 1930.
A law of 1924 encourages tea around Rize, plantations follow after 1937, and the first tea factory opens there in 1947. Today Turkey drinks more tea per person than any other country.
The name *Türk* enters written history with a nomadic empire of Inner Asia that Chinese sources call Tujue. Over the following centuries, Turkic-speaking groups move west across the steppe.

*Van kahvaltısı*, with herb cheese and *murtuğa*, becomes a registered geographical indication: one of the regional versions of *kahvaltı*, the Turkish breakfast, whose name comes from *kahve altı*, before coffee.
Ramazan Bayramı and Kurban Bayramı, the two great holidays of Islam, are also the great family occasions of the year in Turkey. They follow the moon and come about eleven days earlier every year.
Mimar Sinan builds the Haseki Hürrem Sultan Hamamı beside Hagia Sophia, one of the public baths he built in Istanbul that are still in use.
The four national days recall the landing at Samsun (19 May 1919), the first Assembly in Ankara (23 April 1920), the battle near Dumlupınar (30 August 1922) and the Republic (29 October 1923).
Istanbul's first public coffeehouses open; two men from Aleppo and Damascus are said to have opened the first, in Tahtakale. In 2013 UNESCO lists Turkish coffee culture.
On 29 October, after the War of Independence and the Treaty of Lausanne, the Grand National Assembly in Ankara proclaims the Republic of Turkey and elects Mustafa Kemal its first president.

Tales of Keloğlan, the bald boy, were passed on by word of mouth for centuries. The Hungarian Turkologist Ignác Kúnos, among the first to write such tales down from storytellers, publishes his collections from 1889.
From the 4th century, Christian hermits and then monks settle among Cappadocia's fairy chimneys, and around Göreme they carve hundreds of churches and chapels out of the rock.
The historian Peçuylu İbrahim notes that some coffeehouse customers play backgammon and chess. The *kahvehane* is still the home of *tavla* and *okey* today.

In the legend told by Turkey's Ministry of Culture, forty soldiers of the Ottoman prince Süleyman Pasha wrestle near Samona in 1346. Since 1924 the Kırkpınar tournament has been held at Sarayiçi, beside Edirne.
The first local brand of *kolonya* appears. Cologne had reached the Ottoman Empire from Europe earlier in the century, and hosts still offer it to every guest's hands.
UNESCO inscribes the spring celebration Hıdrellez, kept on the night of 5 to 6 May, as a joint file of Turkey and North Macedonia.
Geographers at the First Geography Congress, in Ankara, divide Turkey into seven regions by landforms, climate, plants, farming and settlement: the regions on this page's map.
People raise huge T-shaped limestone pillars at Göbekli Tepe, near Şanlıurfa, some 6,000 years before Stonehenge. UNESCO adds the site to the World Heritage List in 2018.
UNESCO makes Gaziantep a Creative City of Gastronomy, and Hatay follows in 2017: two stops on Turkey's map of dishes, from Adana kebab to Black Sea *hamsi* and Aegean olive oil.

Around 1300 Osman leads one of the small principalities of north-western Anatolia. His dynasty rules for more than six centuries, from Bursa, Edirne and then Istanbul, until the sultanate is abolished in 1922.
Mehmed II's first covered market hall, the Cevahir Bedesteni, is finished a few years after 1453. The Grand Bazaar grows around it: today more than sixty streets and about four thousand shops.
On 26 August the army of Sultan Alp Arslan meets the Byzantine army at Malazgirt (Manzikert), north of Lake Van; Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes loses the battle and is taken prisoner.
Between the Treaty of Passarowitz and the revolt of 1730, Istanbul builds palaces and gardens such as Sadabad, and İbrahim Müteferrika's press prints its first book in 1729.
Evliya Çelebi is born in Istanbul. He travels from Bosnia to Baghdad and from Crimea to Egypt, as far as Vienna, and tells it all in the ten volumes of his *Seyahatname*.
events.abroad: from Bosnia to Baghdad, from Crimea to Egypt

events.text: By the 16th century Karagöz shadow theatre is already a highly developed art. A legend makes its two heroes workers on a mosque in Bursa, in the time of Orhan Gazi.
Rumi's family settles in Konya, the Seljuk capital, in 1228. There Mevlânâ writes the *Mesnevi*, in Persian, and dies on 17 December 1273.
Yunus Emre, a dervish of the Sufi path, writes poems in plain Anatolian Turkish. For seven hundred years people have read and sung them.
The son of Celsus, a Roman governor of Asia, builds the library at Ephesus in his father's honour. Over the centuries the city's harbour silts up; excavations begin in 1895.

After a siege that began on 6 April, Mehmed II's army takes Constantinople on 29 May, known in Turkish as *İstanbul'un Fethi* and in English often as the fall of Constantinople. It becomes the Ottoman capital.
UNESCO lists Turkish coffee culture and tradition, and its description names reading the grounds, *kahve falı*, as part of it. Nobody knows exactly how old the practice is.
Mimar Sinan, past eighty, builds the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne for Selim II, the work he himself considered his most important. UNESCO lists it in 2011.
Stones raised in the Orkhon valley for the Göktürk prince Kül Tigin and his brother Bilge Kağan carry the oldest long texts known in any Turkic language. Vilhelm Thomsen deciphers them in 1893.
The oldest manuscripts of the Book of Dede Korkut, twelve Oghuz tales long told by word of mouth, date from the 15th or 16th century. A third copy turns up in northern Iran in 2018.
The Ottoman sailor Piri Reis finishes a world map on gazelle skin at Gelibolu. The surviving part shows the Atlantic with the coasts of Europe, Africa and South America.
From the 16th century, meddahs grow in number: storytellers who play every character alone, with a handkerchief and a stick, in coffeehouses, markets and the palace.
The first town rises on the mound of Hisarlık near the Dardanelles. Its nine main layers span some 4,000 years, and their link to Homer's Troy is still debated.
Women win the vote in stages: in municipal elections in 1930, in villages in 1933, for parliament in 1934. In the election of February 1935, 17 women become deputies.
On 13 October the Grand National Assembly makes Ankara, then a town of about 20,000 people, the capital. A planned city follows, laid out after a competition won by Hermann Jansen in 1927.
A court record of Üsküdar sets the weight and price of *simit*. Simit, fish sandwiches and stuffed mussels are still sold from Istanbul's trays, carts and boats.
İznik's potters begin making fritware. In the 16th century their tiles cover the walls of Mimar Sinan's mosques, in cobalt blue, turquoise and, from the 1550s, a raised red.
Beşiktaş (1903), Galatasaray (1905) and Fenerbahçe (1907) are founded in Istanbul, and the first Galatasaray–Fenerbahçe match, later called the Intercontinental Derby, is played on 17 January 1909.
Yeşilçam, named after a street in Beyoğlu, makes two hundred or more films a year at its height. Since the 2000s, Turkish TV series have been sold to more than a hundred countries.
Pir Sultan Abdal is thought to live in Banaz, a village of Sivas: one of the âşıks, poets who travel with their *saz*. UNESCO lists the tradition in 2009.
People live at Çatalhöyük, on the Konya plain, in mud-brick houses without doors, entered by a ladder through the roof. UNESCO lists the site in 2012.
King Labarna moves the Hittite capital to Hattusa, near today's Boğazkale. Its archive of about 25,000 clay tablets reveals the oldest known Indo-European language.
Takiyüddin's observatory in Istanbul makes regular observations from 1577, among them that year's great comet, until it is pulled down on the sultan's order on 22 January 1580.
Fuzuli, in Iraq, and Baki, in Istanbul, write gazels: Divan poetry, the poetry of the Ottoman court and cities. Nedim follows in the early 18th century.
A wedding still often begins with the *kız isteme* and its salted coffee, and the *kına gecesi*, the henna night, comes a day or two before the ceremony.
During Ramadan about three thousand drummers wake Istanbul's 961 neighbourhoods for *sahur*; a few still sing manis at the door. Manis are still sung in Kars, Erzurum and Ardahan too.
From Halide Edib's *Ateşten Gömlek* (1922) to Orhan Pamuk's Nobel Prize (2006), five writers tell Turkey's 20th century: Halide Edib, Sabahattin Ali, Sait Faik, Yaşar Kemal and Pamuk.
By one account the first *dolmuş* lines open in Istanbul, from Karaköy to Beyoğlu and from Eminönü to Taksim, at ten kuruş a passenger: shared taxis that leave when they are full.
*Takvim-i Vekâyi*, the Ottoman state's official newspaper, first appears on 1 November. *Tercüman-ı Ahvâl*, the first private newspaper published by Turks, follows in 1860.
From *Telemak* (1862), counted as the first novel translated into Turkish, to Halit Ziya's *Aşk-ı Memnu* as a book (1901), the novel reaches Turkish readers, mostly as newspaper serials.
The *Türk Dili Tetkik Cemiyeti*, later the *Türk Dil Kurumu*, is founded on 12 July, and the first Turkish Language Congress meets at Dolmabahçe Palace on 26 September.
Kaşgarlı Mahmud writes the *Dîvânu Lugâti't-Türk*, a dictionary of the Turkic languages of his time with about 290 proverbs. Its only manuscript resurfaces in Istanbul in 1912.
Teodor Kasap starts *Diyojen*, a weekly humour magazine, in Istanbul on 24 November. A long line of satirical papers follows, down to *Gırgır* and *Leman*.
The Translation Bureau meets for the first time in Ankara on 28 February. By one count, about 866 works from twenty languages are translated into Turkish by 1966.
